## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r cars}
summary(cars)
```

## Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r pressure, echo=FALSE}
plot(pressure)
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

```{R data table file}

library(data.table)
data_url <- "https://goo.gl/uQguPg"
system.time(nycflights <- fread(data_url))
# user  system elapsed
#   0.372   0.092   1.250
```

```{}
# fread is much faster than read.table, and gets faster as the data get bigger
system.time(trash <- read.table(data_url, sep=",", head=T))
# user  system elapsed
#   1.595   0.136   4.239
```

# the print() method works better than for data.frames too!
nycflights
class(nycflights)

# simple subsetting, note that we can refer to variables by name
# no need to use nycflights$origin or nycflights$month (but that would work)
# also don't need the comma like w/ data.frames (though that'd be fine!)
nycflights[origin == "JFK" & month == 6L] # all flights originating at JFK in June
nycflights[10:15] # rows 10 through 15

# order by origin in ascending order and then month in descending order
# note we can use "-" to get descending order on month
# order() actually uses forder() which is faster than base::order()
nycflights[order(origin, -month)]

# get the month variable as a vector
tmp <- nycflights[, month]
class(tmp)

# get the month variable as a data.table
nycflights[, .(month)]
nycflights[, list(month)] # same thing
class(tmp)

# get month and origin as a data.table
# note that we can use .() instead of list(), they mean the same thing for DT
tmp <- nycflights[, .(month, origin)]

# another DT with a few columns, this time with two of the three renamed
tmp <- nycflights[, .(airline = carrier, tailnumber = tailnum, origin)]

# .N is a special n

# .N is a code for "the number of rows in the DT"
# compute number of flights with no arrival or departure delay
nycflights[, sum(arr_delay <= 0 & dep_delay <= 0)]
nycflights[arr_delay <= 0 & dep_delay <= 0, .N] # alternative method
# fraction of flights had no delays:
nycflights[, sum(arr_delay <= 0 & dep_delay <= 0) / .N]
nycflights[, sum(arr_delay <= 0 & dep_delay <= 0) / nrow(nycflights)] # same same

# putting it together: compute average arrival and departure delay for all flights
# leaving JFK in June
nycflights[origin == "JFK" & month == 6L, .(mean_arr_delay=mean(arr_delay), mean_dep_delay=mean(dep_delay))]

# how many flights left JFK in June?
nycflights[origin == "JFK" & month == 6L, .N]

# these are the same, but "with=FALSE" allows you to use data.frame style
nycflights[, .(arr_delay, dep_delay)]
nycflights[, c("arr_delay", "dep_delay"), with=FALSE]

# using by
# how many flights from each origin airport?
nycflights[, .N, by=origin]
# nrow(nycflights[origin == "JFK"])
# nrow(nycflights[origin == "EWR"])
# nrow(nycflights[origin == "LGA"])

# number of June flights and mean departure delay by origin airport
nycflights[month == 6L, .(.N, mean(dep_delay)), by=origin]
nycflights[month == 6, .(.N, mean(dep_delay)), by=origin]

# mean arrival delay by month
nycflights[, .(mean(dep_delay)), by=month]
plot(nycflights[, .(mean_dep_delay=mean(dep_delay)), by=month], pch=16, cex=2, col="tomato")

# total number of trips by American Airlines for each origin-dest pair
nycflights[carrier == "AA", .N, by=.(origin, dest)]

# mean departure and arrival delays for AA by origin, dest, month
nycflights[carrier == "AA", .(mean(dep_delay), mean(arr_delay)), by=.(origin, dest, month)]

# chaining: number of AA flights by origin and destination, ordered by inc(origin) and dec(dest)
nycflights[carrier == "AA", .N, by=.(origin, dest)][order(origin, -dest)]
# DT[i1, j1, by1][i2, j2, by2]

# by can also accept expressions!
# number of flights that departed/arrived early/late
nycflights[, .N, by=.(dep_delay > 0, arr_delay > 0)]

# using .SD and .SDcols
# compute the mean of ALL columns for AA for each origin-destination pair

nycflights[carrier == "AA", lapply(.SD, mean), by=.(origin, dest)]
nycflights[carrier == "AA", lapply(.SD, base::mean), by=.(origin, dest)]

# do it again, but just the means for arr_delay, dep_delay, and distance
nycflights[carrier == "AA", lapply(.SD, mean), by=.(origin, dest), .SDcols=c("arr_delay", "dep_delay", "distance")]
# nycflights[carrier == "AA", lapply(.SD, mean), by=.(origin, dest), .SDcols=c(arr_delay, dep_delay, distance)]

# calculating new variables in place
names(nycflights)
nycflights[, total_delay := arr_delay + dep_delay]
nycflights[, .(avg_speed = distance / air_time)] # this doesn't create a variable, but it does calculate it!
nycflights[, avg_speed := distance / air_time]

# a more advanced example
LinearSlope <- function(x, y){
  lm1 <- lm(y ~ x)
  return(summary(lm1)$r.squared)
}

# how much variation in air_time does distance explain for each carrier?
nycflights[, .(speed_corr=LinearSlope(air_time, distance)), by=carrier][order(speed_corr)]
# note the difference here, adding that variable preserves the size of the data.table
# so we end up repeating a lot of the values of speed_corr
nycflights[, speed_corr := LinearSlope(air_time, distance), by=carrier]

```
